title: What happens if a message exceeds the default size (RecordTooLargeException), and how do you support larger messages?
shortTitle: What happens if a message exceeds the default size (RecordTooLargeException), and how do you support larger messages?
topicTitle: What happens if a message exceeds the default size

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka enforces a maximum record size at several layers. The producer rejects a record larger than `max.request.size` (default one megabyte) by throwing `RecordTooLargeException` before anything is sent. The broker independently rejects batches larger than `message.max.bytes`, and the topic can override this with `max.message.bytes`. The consumer must also be able to fetch the batch, bounded by `max.partition.fetch.bytes` and `fetch.max.bytes`. To support larger payloads you either raise all these limits consistently, enable compression, or use the claim-check pattern where the large blob goes to object storage and only a reference travels through Kafka.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's mailroom only accepts envelopes up to a certain thickness. If a clerk tries to post a two-hundred-page loan agreement in one envelope, the mailroom refuses it at the counter before it ever leaves the branch. To send something big you can either officially raise the thickness limit at every checkpoint, compress the pages, or put the big document in the vault and mail only a claim ticket that says where to find it.
s1_definition.oneliner: The producer throws RecordTooLargeException above one megabyte, and you fix it by raising the limits at every layer, compressing, or sending a claim-check reference instead of the blob.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka enforces a maximum record size at several layers. The producer rejects a record larger than `max.request.size` (default one megabyte) by throwing `RecordTooLargeException` before anything is sent. The broker independently rejects batches larger than `message.max.bytes`, and the topic can override this with `max.message.bytes`. The consumer must also be able to fetch the batch, bounded by `max.partition.fetch.bytes` and `fetch.max.bytes`. To support larger payloads you either raise all these limits consistently, enable compression, or use the claim-check pattern where the large blob goes to object storage and only a reference travels through Kafka.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's mailroom only accepts envelopes up to a certain thickness. If a clerk tries to post a two-hundred-page loan agreement in one envelope, the mailroom refuses it at the counter before it ever leaves the branch. To send something big you can either officially raise the thickness limit at every checkpoint, compress the pages, or put the big document in the vault and mail only a claim ticket that says where to find it.

**One line to remember:** The producer throws RecordTooLargeException above one megabyte, and you fix it by raising the limits at every layer, compressing, or sending a claim-check reference instead of the blob.

sections.s2_technical:
The one-megabyte default appears in multiple places and all of them matter. On the producer, `max.request.size` defaults to 1048576 bytes. If your serialized record is bigger, the producer fails fast with `RecordTooLargeException` and nothing is sent, so you get an immediate, local error rather than a mysterious broker rejection. You can raise it with `props.put("max.request.size", 5242880)` for five megabytes.

On the broker, `message.max.bytes` is the cluster-wide ceiling and the topic-level `max.message.bytes` can override it per topic. If a batch exceeds the broker limit, the broker rejects the produce request and the producer sees the error. A classic mistake is raising only the producer limit and forgetting the broker, which still rejects the write. You set the topic limit with `kafka-configs --alter --topic statements --add-config max.message.bytes=5242880`.

On the consumer, `max.partition.fetch.bytes` bounds how much one partition can return in a single fetch, and `fetch.max.bytes` bounds the whole fetch. If these are smaller than your largest record, the consumer cannot make progress and effectively stalls, so when you raise producer and broker limits you must also raise `props.put("max.partition.fetch.bytes", 5242880)`.

Beyond raising limits, compression helps a lot. Setting `props.put("compression.type", "zstd")` compresses the batch on the producer, and because many banking payloads such as JSON statements are highly compressible, a five-megabyte statement can shrink well under a megabyte. The broker stores and ships the compressed batch, and the consumer decompresses it, so compression saves network and disk end to end.

The senior recommendation for genuinely large payloads such as PDF statements or cheque images is the claim-check pattern. You upload the blob to object storage like Amazon S3, then publish a small Kafka message containing the bucket, key, checksum, and size. The consumer reads the reference and downloads the blob. This keeps Kafka fast because large objects never clog the partitions, keeps retention cheap, and lets you lifecycle-manage big files separately. The tradeoff is an extra round trip to object storage and the need to handle the case where the blob is deleted before the consumer reads it.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India generates monthly account statements. For Rajesh (SAV2001) a normal statement is small, but for Priya (CUR3001), a property owner with thousands of rent transactions, the statement can be several megabytes.

Problem 1 — the statement service tries to publish Priya's big statement to Kafka and the producer throws `RecordTooLargeException` immediately, so the message is never sent and the downstream email service never gets it.

Problem 2 — simply raising the producer limit is not enough because the broker still rejects anything over its own `message.max.bytes`, and even if the write succeeds the consumer with a small fetch limit cannot read it back.

Problem 3 — raising limits everywhere makes the cluster slower and riskier for truly huge files. This is exactly what the claim-check pattern solves: the big statement PDF goes to object storage and only a tiny reference message flows through Kafka.

The code will show the failing large publish, a corrected version that compresses and sizes the record, and the claim-check approach where only a reference is published.

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: broker1:9092
    producer:
      properties:
        max.request.size: 5242880      # 5 MB, raised from 1 MB default
        compression.type: zstd         # shrink highly compressible JSON/PDF text
    consumer:
      properties:
        max.partition.fetch.bytes: 5242880   # must be able to read the larger record
# Topic side (set via CLI, shown here for reference):
# kafka-configs --alter --topic statements --add-config max.message.bytes=5242880
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Raise the TOPIC limit too, otherwise the broker still rejects large records
kafka-configs --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 --alter \
  --topic statements --add-config max.message.bytes=5242880

# Run
java -cp target/statement-publisher-service-1.0.0.jar \
  com.bank.statement.StatementPublisherDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya's monthly statement, roughly three megabytes of JSON.

Step 1 — with default limits, the producer serializes the statement, measures it at three megabytes, and immediately throws `RecordTooLargeException` because it is above the one-megabyte `max.request.size`. Nothing leaves the producer.

Step 2 — with the producer limit raised to five megabytes and `zstd` compression enabled, the producer compresses the highly repetitive JSON down to a few hundred kilobytes and sends it. Because the topic's `max.message.bytes` was also raised, the broker accepts it.

Step 3 — the broker stores the compressed batch on disk. A consumer with a matching `max.partition.fetch.bytes` fetches and decompresses it, getting the full statement back.

Step 4 — in the claim-check path, the service uploads the PDF to S3 and publishes only a small reference message with the S3 URI, size, and checksum. This message is tiny, so it sails through even the default limits. The consumer reads the reference and downloads the blob from S3.

```
2026-10-24 21:30:01 [SEVERE] Rejected at default 1 MB limit: The message is 3000064 bytes when serialized which is larger than 1048576.
2026-10-24 21:30:02 [INFO] Large statement published (compressed) offset 12
2026-10-24 21:30:02 [INFO] Claim-check reference published (tiny) offset 13
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Statement Service: Priya (CUR3001) statement ~3 MB JSON
    │
    ├─ PATH A: default limits                ├─ PATH B: raised + compressed
    │   producer measures 3 MB               │   max.request.size = 5 MB
    │   > max.request.size (1 MB)            │   compression.type = zstd → ~300 KB
    │   ✗ RecordTooLargeException            │   broker max.message.bytes = 5 MB ✓
    │   nothing sent                         │   stored compressed on disk
    │                                        │   consumer fetch 5 MB → decompress
    │                                        ▼
    │                                   full statement delivered
    │
    └─ PATH C: claim-check (best for huge blobs)
        upload PDF → s3://bank-statements/CUR3001/2026-10.pdf
        publish tiny reference {uri,size,checksum}  (< 1 KB)
        consumer reads ref → downloads from S3
        ▼
      Kafka stays fast, big blob lives in object storage
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka enforces a size limit at several layers, and the default is one megabyte. On the producer, the maximum request size defaults to one megabyte, so if I try to publish anything bigger it fails immediately with a record-too-large exception before anything is sent. On the broker, the maximum message bytes setting is an independent ceiling, and the topic can override it. On the consumer, the per-partition fetch bytes must also be large enough to read the record back.

To support larger messages I have three options. The first is to raise the limits consistently at the producer, the topic, and the consumer, because raising only one of them leaves the others rejecting or stalling. The second is to enable compression, which is very effective for banking payloads like JSON statements because they are highly repetitive, so a multi-megabyte statement can shrink well under a megabyte and the broker stores and ships the smaller compressed batch.

The third and best option for genuinely large files is the claim-check pattern. I upload the blob, such as a PDF statement or a cheque image, to object storage, and then I publish only a small reference message with the storage location, size, and checksum. The consumer reads the reference and downloads the blob. This keeps Kafka fast and cheap because large objects never clog the partitions.

In my National Bank of India project, Priya's monthly statement could reach several megabytes because she has thousands of rent transactions. We used compression for moderately sized statements and the claim-check pattern for the large PDF files, uploading them to object storage and sending only a reference through Kafka. That kept the cluster healthy while still letting the email service attach the full statement.
